paras: The assault on Robert Hamlin was an attack by striking teamsters on Robert J. Hamlin, a Black non-union coal-wagon driver, at Washington and Dey streets in New York City on September 9, 1903. Hamlin was beaten with a shovel and chased by a large crowd, and two members of the Teamsters' Union, Robert Nelligan and James O'Brien, were later convicted and sentenced to nine months in the penitentiary. The Sun followed it from the street to the sentence as a case of union violence against a man's right to work.

The teamsters of Curtis & Blaisdell, coal dealers, had struck after the firm refused a union order to let its drivers off on Labor Day to march in a parade. The firm hired about eighty non-union drivers, Hamlin among them, while strikers hooted at the new men as "scab."

Shortly after noon on September 9, as Hamlin drove a coal wagon back to the firm's Washington street yard, one man stopped his horses and two others climbed to the seat and ordered him down. Hamlin later testified that the two defendants had yelled "Scab! Scab!" and that one beat him on the head with a shovel from the wagon.

Hamlin then drew a revolver, which he said his employers had advised him to carry, and fired into the air. He galloped off toward West street with a crowd the Sun put at "fully a thousand" behind him and ran into the Hoboken ferry house. Patrolman Filan, who thought a murder had been committed, arrested him there. The policeman later testified that the crowd chasing Hamlin, with Nelligan and O'Brien, yelled "Kill the nigger!"; Hamlin's injuries were reported as not serious.

On Hamlin's word the patrolman arrested O'Brien and Nelligan, and Magistrate Pool held them for examination, while Hamlin was charged with carrying a concealed weapon and paroled. The next day Hamlin recognized a third striker, John Deveey, among the spectators, and Pool held him in $500 bail after refusing his lawyer's offer of a union guarantee. No report of Deveey's later disposition or of the outcome of the weapons charge against Hamlin was found.

At their December trial before Recorder Goff, the prosecutor pressed Nelligan on whether the two had been sent to do picket duty, which he denied. The jury convicted them on December 22, and on December 24 Goff sentenced each to nine months in the penitentiary for assault in the second degree, saying he was being merciful in not sending them to state prison.

All of the coverage found appeared in the New York Sun, and no account in the Black press was found. The Sun's first story, headed "STRIKERS BEAT A DRIVER," described a "mob" and a "man hunt" in West street and called the assailants "a band of husky strikers." Its trial report opened with the irony that Hamlin had been "impertinent enough to take a job" vacated by union order, and its verdict story ran under the headline "UNION SLUGGERS CONVICTED."

The paper identified Hamlin as "a negro" but framed the case as union lawlessness, printing at length Goff's statement that the right to strike carried other men's right to work. The crowd's racial epithet surfaced only in the policeman's trial testimony.

The defendants told the jury that they had only called Hamlin a "scab" and urged him to quit, that he fired at them, twice according to Nelligan and once according to O'Brien, and that they then tried to close with him. Hamlin said he fired once into the air, the first report said twice, and the policeman said Hamlin told him he had fired at the two men in self-defence. The sentencing story dated the assault September 7, against September 9 in the first report and the trial coverage, and the bail first given as $2,000 each appeared as $1,000 each the next day.

bases: Striking union teamsters attacked a non-union Black driver hired to replace them during a strike against a coal firm (A3, A4, A7).

accounts.label: Sun first-day report
accounts.gist: A band of strikers stopped Hamlin's team, two climbed up, knocked him into the wagon and beat him with an iron shovel; he fired two shots in the air and fled with a crowd of about a thousand behind him.

accounts.label: Hamlin and Flood at trial
accounts.gist: The defendants yelled 'Scab!', climbed on the wagon, and one beat Hamlin on the head with a shovel; he fired one shot in the air to scare them and ran when about five hundred men came at him.

accounts.label: Policeman Finlan at trial
accounts.gist: He saw Hamlin chased by Nelligan, O'Brien and a crowd yelling 'Kill the nigger!'; Hamlin told him he had fired at the two men in self-defence, and one cartridge was spent.

accounts.label: Defendants' version
accounts.gist: Nelligan and O'Brien said they only called Hamlin a 'scab' and urged him to quit; Hamlin fired at them (twice per Nelligan, once per O'Brien) and they then tried to close with him.

framing.detail: The Sun headlined 'STRIKERS BEAT A DRIVER' and 'UNION SLUGGERS CONVICTED', mocked the charge that Hamlin was 'impertinent enough to take a job', and printed Recorder Goff's right-to-work remarks at length; the attack was treated as union lawlessness, with race noted but not discussed.

conflicts.note: The same-day-after report and the trial testimony give Sept. 9; the sentencing story's Sept. 7 stands alone.
